title: From Scene to Story: A Workshop on Narrative Craft

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's workshop is about the craft of narrative — specifically, how to turn a simple scene into a compelling piece of writing. We'll look at three things: how you open, how you control time, and how you close.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Let's start with the opening. The first sentence of a narrative does several jobs simultaneously. It establishes voice, sets tone, and — most importantly — creates a question in the reader's mind. That question is what keeps them reading. Without a question, there is no pull.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Consider this opening: "She had not been back to the village in fifteen years." Notice what this does. The past perfect "had not been" immediately signals that something has changed. The reader asks: why did she leave? Why is she back now? Two questions from seven words. That is good craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Now let's talk about controlling time. The biggest mistake developing writers make is treating time as a straight line. Real narrative time is elastic. Some moments expand — you slow down and show every detail. Other moments compress — you skip years in a sentence. The skill is knowing which moments deserve expansion and which deserve compression.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: A moment deserves expansion when it is emotionally significant. The first time two characters meet. The moment before a crucial decision. These deserve time. A moment deserves compression when it is necessary but not meaningful. "Three years passed." "She grew used to the silence." These are compression sentences.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Now, narrative tenses are your tools for controlling time. Past simple moves time forward. Past continuous freezes time and adds texture. Past perfect moves time backward. Think of them as camera techniques: the past simple is a cut, the past continuous is a slow pan, the past perfect is a flashback.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: The third element is the closing. A good closing resonates — it gives the reader something to take away. Weak closings often just stop. Strong closings echo the opening, resolve the central question (or deepen it), or shift the reader's understanding of everything they have read. The best endings feel both surprising and inevitable — exactly like a great character.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Here is a simple exercise for today. Take any single sentence — your opening line — and ask: what question does this create? If you cannot answer that question, rewrite the sentence. Then write three more sentences to begin your story: one in the past continuous to set the scene, one in the past simple for the first action, and one in the past perfect to hint at the backstory. Four sentences. A beginning.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Aldanova
dialogue.text: Great writing is not about finding perfect sentences. It is about making choices — about what to show, what to hide, what to slow down, and what to speed through. Those choices are what create meaning. Now — open your notebooks.
